purpose: First hands-on TypeScript practice project — migrated a vanilla JS link generator tool to TypeScript

lessons.summary: Browsers cannot run .ts files at all. TypeScript is a separate compiler (tsc) that reads .ts source, checks types statically, then deletes all type annotations and writes plain .js. Only the compiled .js is ever shipped/deployed/run — the .ts source and the whole TS toolchain never reach end users.
keyFacts: Type annotations (e.g. ': string', ': void') are completely ERASED at compile time — they produce zero runtime code and zero runtime checks.
Verification happens once, when you run `tsc` / `npm run build` — never while the code is actually running.

Non-null assertions (!) and type assertions (as Type) are just promises made to the compiler — they generate no real runtime check; if wrong, you still get a runtime crash, TS just stops warning you about it at compile time.

lessons.summary: How to add TypeScript tooling to an existing vanilla JS project.
steps: npm install --save-dev typescript  → installs TS locally (devDependency), not globally, so the exact version is pinned per-project via package-lock.json
Add "build": "tsc" under package.json's "scripts", then run with npm run build
Add node_modules to .gitignore (regenerable from package.json + package-lock.json, shouldn't be committed)
Rename scripts.js → scripts.ts; index.html keeps pointing at scripts.js (the compiled OUTPUT), never at scripts.ts

lessons.summary: document.getElementById() returns HTMLElement | null in TS, because the compiler can't know at compile time whether an element with that ID really exists in the HTML.
options: Non-null assertion: document.getElementById('x')! — tells the compiler 'trust me, not null'. No runtime check. Chosen for this project: small personal project, both files controlled by the same person.
Safer alternative: if (!el) throw new Error(...) — actually checks at runtime too, better for team/production code.

lessons.summary: document.getElementById() returns the generic HTMLElement type, which lacks properties like .value that only exist on specific subtypes.
lessons.syntaxRule: `as Type` goes right after the EXPRESSION whose type you're asserting, never next to the variable name on the left of `=`.

lessons.summary: Restrict a value to an exact fixed set of string values instead of the generic `string` type, catching typos at compile time instead of causing silent runtime bugs.
lessons.example:
type ServerOption = "APP" | "DO" | "OVH";
let mySelectValue = mySelect.value as ServerOption;
lessons.verifiedBehavior: Deliberately introducing a typo (e.g. case "OHV":) produced compiler error ts(2678): 'Type is not comparable to type ServerOption' — proven the union catches mistakes that plain `string` would silently accept.

lessons.summary: `type Name = ...` always creates a type alias — a reusable name for ANY type, not just unions.
commonUses: Object shapes: type User = { name: string; age: number };
Primitive aliasing for documentation: type UserId = string;

lessons.summary: Utility type that generates an object type requiring exactly the keys in union K, each with value type V. Shorthand for manually writing out { key1: V; key2: V; ... }.
lessons.whyItMattersOverAPlainObject: Record<K,V> stays LINKED to the union type K. If K gains a new member later and you forget to add the matching key to the Record-typed object, TS errors immediately ('Property missing'). A manually-typed object literal or an untyped/inferred object has NO such connection — it silently goes stale.
lessons.appliedRefactor: Replaced a 3-case switch statement (which repeated the entire URL template 3 times) with one Record lookup (serverDomains[mySelectValue]) + a single template literal construction — single source of truth for the URL shape.

lessons.topic: Explicit function parameter and return types
lessons.summary: Annotate function signatures explicitly, and use them as a forcing function to deduplicate near-identical functions.
lessons.appliedRefactor: 3 near-duplicate copy-to-clipboard functions (copyIPClickListener, copyBtnClickListener, copyCdnBtnClickListener) reduced to thin wrappers that extract .innerText from their specific element and call the one shared copyToClipboard(text) function.
lessons.bonusFind: Caught and fixed a variable-shadowing bug during the refactor — a local `const resultLink` inside one of the old functions was shadowing the outer `let resultLink` (which held the generated URL); renamed to resultLinkText.

lessons.summary: Both mean 'could be any type', but they behave oppositely for safety.
lessons.any: Disables type checking completely for that value. You can do ANYTHING with it (call missing methods, access missing properties) with zero compiler complaint, even if it will crash at runtime.
lessons.unknown: Also means 'could be anything', but TS REFUSES to let you use any property/method on it until you narrow/prove its actual type first (e.g. with `instanceof`, `typeof`).
lessons.empiricalFinding: Promise.prototype.catch()'s reject-callback parameter is typed `any` by TypeScript's standard lib (confirmed via editor hover) — NOT `unknown`. The `unknown` default only applies to synchronous try/catch blocks under `strict` mode, not to Promise .catch() callbacks.
lessons.experimentProof: With (err: any) [default], `err.message` compiled with ZERO warning even though err might not have .message. After annotating explicitly as (err: unknown), the same line failed to compile (ts(18046): 'err' is of type 'unknown') until wrapped in an `instanceof Error` check.

lessons.topic: Module system config gotcha (real runtime bug)
lessons.summary: A plain browser <script> with no bundler and no import/export statements broke with `Uncaught ReferenceError: exports is not defined` after compiling.
lessons.rootCause: tsconfig.json's default `"moduleDetection": "force"` forced TypeScript to treat the file as a module even without any import/export, and `"module": "nodenext"` resolved to CommonJS output (since package.json had no "type": "module"), so tsc injected Node.js-style module boilerplate (`Object.defineProperty(exports, ...)`) that doesn't exist in a browser.
lessons.fix: Leave "moduleDetection" on its default "auto" (comment it out) so TS correctly detects the file has no import/export and treats it as a plain script — the "module" setting then becomes irrelevant for this file regardless of its value.
lessons.deprecationNote: "module": "none" seemed like the semantically 'correct' explicit choice, but it is DEPRECATED and will be removed in TypeScript 7.0 — don't use it. The real fix was always about moduleDetection, not about which module value was chosen.

lessons.summary: tsc can generate extra files beyond the compiled .js depending on tsconfig options.

files.scripts.d.ts + scripts.d.ts.map: Generated by "declaration": true + "declarationMap": true. Contains only type signatures for other TS projects to import as a library. Since this script has zero exports, the file was always empty — disabled both options, since this project is not a reusable library.
files.scripts.js.map: Generated by "sourceMap": true. Maps the compiled .js back to the original .ts source so browser DevTools can show/debug the original TypeScript file instead of the compiled JS. Purely a local development convenience; should never be uploaded to production. Disabled for this project to keep deploy simple.

lessons.gotcha: tsc never deletes stale output files from a previous config — after disabling declaration/declarationMap, the old scripts.d.ts and scripts.d.ts.map had to be deleted manually.

lessons.topic: Deployment checklist for a plain static TS-compiled site
lessons.workflowReminder: Editing scripts.ts or tsconfig.json has ZERO effect on a running Live Server / deployed page until `npm run build` re-runs — the server just serves whatever scripts.js already exists on disk. Always: edit → npm run build → refresh/redeploy.
lessons.futureIdea: Consider `tsc --watch` later for auto-recompiling on save during local development.

mentorNotes.teachingStyle: Guided Socratic questions, learner writes all code himself, mentor never writes/edits the actual code.
commonSyntaxMistakes: Placing `as Type` next to the variable name instead of right after the expression.
Writing a type on the right side of `=` instead of after `:` (e.g. trying `let x = Record<K,V>` instead of `let x: Record<K,V> = {...}`).
Taking meta-notation placeholders like `<domain>` (meaning 'fill in here') as literal syntax, leaving stray `<`/`>` characters in real code.
strengths: Reasons well about real engineering trade-offs when given an explicit choice with consequences (e.g. chose `!` over `if...throw` specifically because it's a small personal project).
Independently caught a variable-shadowing bug during a refactor without being told.
